adds.title: Reforms to remove barriers for LGBTQIA+ community | Western Australian Government
adds.summary: WA Premier Roger Cook and Attorney-General John Quigley announced on 16 April 2024 that the Births, Deaths, Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Bill 2024 would be introduced to State Parliament that week, repealing the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and abolishing the Gender Reassignment Board - which they say makes WA the only remaining Australian jurisdiction with such a board - in favour of a streamlined administrative process via the Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages. Applicants would no longer need medical or surgical reassignment, providing instead a statement from a medical practitioner or psychologist certifying appropriate clinical treatment, which may include counselling; a 'non-binary' sex descriptor would become available, stricter rules apply to under-18s (parental consent or Family Court of WA permission), and the Bill contains a statutory review clause after three years. The announcement implements the WA Law Reform Commission's 2018 recommendations and links the reform to a planned new Equal Opportunity Act and a conversion-practices ban in 2025. This is the official government source for the record's claim that the 2024 Act removes medical and surgical prerequisites for registering a sex or gender change in Western Australia.

adds.title: Equal Opportunity Commission Fact Sheet - Gender Reassigned Person Discrimination | Western Australian Government
adds.summary: The WA Equal Opportunity Commission's fact sheet states that the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 (WA), recently passed with commencement still to be proclaimed, amends the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA) at section 4(1) by deleting the definition of 'gender reassigned person' and inserting a new definition tied to recognition certificates under the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 or registration of sex or gender under the amended regime. It warns the amendment will not operate retrospectively and that 'gender history' discrimination complaints under the Equal Opportunity Act will need to be made in compliance with the new registration requirements once the Act commences, and notes the Act also repeals the Gender Reassignment Act 2000 and the Gender Reassignment Regulations 2001. This primary government document confirms the record's claim that the 2024 reform feeds back into the scope of WA's 'gender history' attribute for complaints purposes and that substantive commencement is by proclamation.

adds.title: How to deal with gender discrimination and transphobia (WA) | Justice Connect
adds.summary: Justice Connect's WA-specific resource (last updated 16 April 2026) states that in Western Australia a discrimination complaint can be made to the WA Commissioner of Equal Opportunity under the Equal Opportunity Act 1984 (WA), with a 12-month lodgement window, an acknowledgment of receipt within one week, and a free conciliation conference as the next step; it also details the alternative federal route - a complaint to the Australian Human Rights Commission under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth) within 24 months (12 months for employment matters) - noting only one route, state or federal, can be chosen. The resource names trans-specific local support in WA (TransFolk of WA, the Freedom Centre for under-26s). This confirms the record's claim that 'gender history' rather than 'gender identity' is the state-level protective attribute in WA and that state complaints run through the Equal Opportunity Commission.

adds.title: Human Rights Act 2004 | Acts | ACT Legislation Register
adds.summary: The official ACT Legislation Register lists the Human Rights Act 2004 (A2004-5) as In Force, with the current republished version and a full republication history back to 1 July 2004, and notes that under section 31 interpreters may consider international law and the judgments of foreign and international courts and tribunals relevant to a human right; it also records uncommenced amendments by the Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025. This is the primary legal source for the record's claim that the ACT has its own Human Rights Act 2004 as the statutory rights framework public authorities must operate within.

adds.title: Serious barriers in accessing health care for Canberra's transgender community highlighted in new study - ABC News
adds.summary: ABC News reported on 16 April 2022 that the ACT government's LGBTIQ+ Health Scoping Study found serious barriers for transgender and gender-diverse Canberrans: a shortage of primary-care professionals, including GPs, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, resulting in 'excessive wait times, delays from referrals and high costs associated with interstate and international travel'. The article records 20 young transgender people on the waitlist of Canberra's only paediatric endocrinologist, some patients waiting a year for an appointment, GP demand rising 20-40 per cent a year, and the study calling the ACT 'the only jurisdiction not to have a comprehensive gender-focused health service' in private practice or through a publicly-funded gender clinic. This is the first documented ACT-specific institutional-capacity finding and qualifies the record's claim that no countervailing region-specific finding was identified for the ACT.

adds.title: LGBTQ conversion therapy banned in Canberra as Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill passes - ABC News
adds.summary: ABC News reported on 27 August 2020 that the ACT Legislative Assembly passed the Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill, so that from early 2021 conversion practices used on protected persons attract up to a 12-month jail term or a $24,000 fine, alongside civil penalties giving the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal power to issue orders and order redress. The bill was amended before passage after the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society argued the definition of conversion practice was 'too broad and vague', while practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition were explicitly not banned. This dated ACT criminal statute supports the record's characterisation of the ACT as a protective rights jurisdiction and adds to the territory's structural positives beyond the Human Rights Act and self-identification custody rule.

adds.title: Radiografía de la educación en diversidad LGTBI+ 2025 - FELGTBI+ / Universidad de Salamanca
adds.summary: FELGTBI+'s September 2025 radiography of LGTBI+ policy (prepared with the Universidad de Salamanca) states that 'Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta y Melilla son los únicos territorios aún sin una ley específica en materia de promoción de los derechos de las personas LGTBI+' - the only Spanish territories still without a specific law on promotion of LGTBI+ rights - and that a 2020 precedent study had placed Ceuta and Melilla at the tail of trans-student recognition and protection rankings. The report notes June 2025 legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias but records no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla. This is the primary national-inventory source for the record's claim that Ceuta appears only as a statutory-gap case with no regional LGTBI or gender-identity statute.

adds.title: Arcópoli pide al Gobierno el traslado "urgente" a la Península de los migrantes LGTBI+ que permanecen en Ceuta - Europa Press
adds.summary: Europa Press reported on 17 September 2026 that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote by letter to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the 'urgent' transfer to the peninsula of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30-31 July, calling transfer 'the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion'. Arcópoli cited the 'extreme vulnerability' of these people, who flee criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those in Ceuta. This is a dated, Ceuta-specific LGTBI episode that grounds the record's claim that Ceuta's border-fence crossing environment creates a distinct document-and-presentation context for LGTBI visitors and migrants.
